name: Overwhelming exception
statement: The overwhelming exception is a generalisation whose stated qualifications remove so many cases that little of the claim is left standing.
meaning: The complaint is about scope rather than truth. Written out in full, the sentence is accurate, and it carries the weight of a much larger claim it no longer makes. The exceptions arrive as a list rather than as a retraction, and the general form is what a reader takes away. David Hackett Fischer, who named it, put it in one line: a generalisation which is a good deal less general than it appears to be. Three Atlas entries sit close to it. The motte-and-bailey fallacy advances a bold claim, retreats to a modest one and returns, which is this fallacy spread over two moves instead of one sentence. No true Scotsman narrows the category so a counterexample stops counting. Special pleading exempts one case from a rule that covers it. The two fallacies about the direction of a generalisation are further away than they look. Hasty generalisation runs from a few cases to a rule, and the fallacy of accident runs from a rule to a case its exceptions should have kept out. Neither describes a claim hollowed out by qualifiers the speaker supplies himself.

origin.where: Historians' Fallacies: Toward a Logic of Historical Thought
origin.note: The name occupies a single page. It is the last of the twelve fallacies in chapter IV, 'Fallacies of Generalization', which runs from page 103, and Fischer's own index of fallacies lists it at 127 and 149. His definition is one sentence and his examples are two. Whether he coined the phrase was not established here, and no earlier source for it was located. The definition that circulates under the name is not his: Wikipedia and Bo Bennett's fallacy list both gloss it as a generalisation that is accurate but carries qualifications eliminating so many cases that the argument is weaker than the arguer implies, wording that appears nowhere in Fischer's text.

evidence: The evidence is textual, and there is little of it. Fischer's page gives the definition and two cases. The first is a joke from 1066 and All That: 'Magna Charta was therefore the chief cause of Democracy in England, and thus a Good Thing for everyone (except the Common People).' The second is an argument by the business historian Gordon C. Bjork, who blamed slow population growth in four American seaport cities between 1790 and 1825 on a failure of foreign trade to expand, having left cotton and re-exports out of his index of trade. Fischer's objection is that the exclusions are not apparent to a casual reader and are vital to the interpretation, and that to make such sweeping exclusions is to make nonsense of the subject. The second indexed occurrence, in a footnote on page 149, is the fuller specimen. Fischer charges C. Vann Woodward with defending the thesis of The Strange Career of Jim Crow through two revisions until it applied to all Southern institutions 'except churches, schools, militia, hotels, restaurants, public buildings, jails, hospitals, asylums, gardens, railroads in several states, and the New Orleans Opera House', and to all Negroes but freedmen, hired slaves, urban Negroes, South Carolina Negroes and in some respects Negro field hands. The name did not travel into the logic textbooks. The string 'overwhelming' appears four times in the fourteenth edition of Copi, Cohen and McMahon's Introduction to Logic, none of them attached to a fallacy, and the phrase occurs in neither Bradley Dowden's list at the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy nor Hans Hansen's Stanford Encyclopedia article nor the taxonomy page of Gary Curtis's Fallacy Files. All four documents were downloaded and searched whole. Where it does live is the online fallacy lists, which is also where its examples come from. Wikipedia's article carries the Monty Python line about what the Romans have done for us and Henry Ford's offer of any colour so long as it is black, and cites Fischer's page 127 for a definition it does not print. Bennett's entry adds a logical form, that claim A is made, numerous exceptions to A are made, therefore A is true.

replication.headline: No study measuring the fallacy was located. The nearest measured question, whether a qualifier attached to a claim reaches the reader at all, has been put to 5,780 people, and single words do not reach them.
replication.detail:
Europe PMC holds two records containing the phrase 'overwhelming exception', a 2020 question-and-answer piece in Seminars in Interventional Radiology and a 2020 PLOS ONE study of law enforcement professionals, and neither concerns the fallacy. Crossref's bibliographic search degrades to loose matching and returns Oxford English Dictionary entries. OpenAlex refused the query for want of account budget and Semantic Scholar returned a rate limit, so that part of the sweep was not completed.

The reader's side of the fallacy has been measured. Van der Bles, van der Linden, Freeman and Spiegelhalter ran four online experiments and one field experiment on the live BBC News website, 5,780 people in total, varying how uncertainty around a published figure was expressed. In experiment 1, on 1,122 people, a numeric range raised how uncertain the figure seemed, d = 0.45 against control, and an explicit verbal statement raised it further, d = 1.17. Experiment 3, on 1,200 people, tested eight formats on a UK unemployment figure. Every one of them raised perceived uncertainty, d = 0.37 to 0.72, except the condition where the single word 'estimated' had been added, which moved nothing at all: M diff = -0.07, P = 1.00. Experiment 4 was preregistered, ran on 1,050 UK adults with a migration figure, and reproduced the pattern with a different word. A numeric range gave d = 0.50, plus or minus notation d = 0.50, and an explicit statement d = 0.68, while writing 'around 101,000' left readers where the control condition left them. Pooling the four studies, the authors' own random-effects meta-analysis puts the effect of communicating uncertainty on perceived uncertainty at d = 0.65, 95% CI [0.42, 0.87], on trust in the numbers at d = -0.34, 95% CI [-0.53, -0.16], and on trust in the source at d = -0.12, 95% CI [-0.22, -0.03]. The BBC field experiment, on 1,531 readers, found the numeric range raised perceived uncertainty by d = 0.19 and changed trust in neither the figure nor the statisticians behind it.

Readers also fail to grade qualifiers finely. Adams and seven colleagues gave people health headlines in six forms and asked them to rank the forms by how causal each was. In the fourth experiment, 380 of 556 recruits survived the exclusions, and the overall ordering was strong, Friedman chi-squared(5) = 900.92, p < .001. Inside the ordering, 'may result in' could not be separated from 'is linked to', p = .08, and its position against 'is associated with' moved between experiments. Their abstract states the general result: participants separate direct cause from can cause from a group of moderate expressions, and do not consistently distinguish within that last group.

Whether the caveat costs the speaker anything has been tested twice by one group, with results that do not line up. Jensen exposed 601 students to one of five cancer news stories, hedged or not. The manipulation registered, M = 4.51 against 3.58 on whether limitations were clear, F(1, 4) = 25.06. Hedging had no main effect on how trustworthy the scientists seemed. It worked only when the caveats were attributed to the researchers themselves, 4.78 against 4.48, F(1, 597) = 7.31, p < .01, and not when attributed to unaffiliated scientists, 4.59 against 4.64, F(1, 597) = 0.21, p = .64. Jensen and six colleagues then ran 1,082 people through four stories. Hedged articles left readers less fatalistic about cancer, F(1, 3) = 12.37, p = .039, r = .11, and refitting the same data with message as a fixed factor reduced that to F(1, 969) = 2.75, p = .09, r = .05. Medical skepticism went the other way between the two analyses, p = .12 with message random and p = .04 with it fixed.

The fine print gives the extreme case, where the qualification is available, covers the reader, and is never opened. Obar and Oeldorf-Hirsch put 500 adults aged over 50 through joining a fictitious social network called NameDrop. 77.6% took the clickwrap and agreed to the privacy policy without opening it. Of the 112 who did open it, the mean time on the page was 69.95 seconds and the median 24.24, against a policy of 7,727 words that would take 26 to 44 minutes to read at the reading speeds they cite. Terms of service ran to 4,741 words, about 16 to 27 minutes, and drew a mean of 81.42 seconds. 91.4% accepted a privacy policy that let NameDrop switch on their camera and pass data to the National Security Agency, and 83.4% accepted terms requiring them to hand over a kidney or other redundant organ in payment. One participant of 500 mentioned the camera clause, none mentioned the agency, and four mentioned the organ.

limits: Nothing here measures the fallacy. It measures what qualifiers do to readers, which is the premise the fallacy rests on rather than the fallacy itself, and none of these researchers set out to test Fischer. The uncertainty experiments manipulate qualifiers around a single number, not exceptions that carve away the scope of a general claim, and the fine-print studies are about a document nobody opens rather than a caveat printed in the sentence. Several documents behind this page were not obtained. Yannis Bakos, Florencia Marotta-Wurgler and David Trossen's study of whether shoppers open software licence agreements is closed at the University of Chicago Press, Unpaywall records no repository copy, and no figure from it appears above. The 2020 NameDrop study is closed at Taylor and Francis on the same test; the figures widely quoted from it, that 74% of 543 undergraduates took the clickwrap and that 98% missed its gotcha clauses, are stated here as the 2022 paper reports them and are not read off the original. Adams and colleagues were read as the author manuscript posted at gwern.net rather than the published article, and that copy is the pre-correction version: the fourth author is missing from it, which is what the American Psychological Association's 2017 correction notice restores. The notice reports no change to any result. Fischer was read as the Internet Archive's OCR text of the first Harper edition, downloaded twice to the same checksum, and the page numbers come from the running heads and his index of fallacies rather than from images of the printed page. Jensen's 2011 paper prints Cohen's d for the fatalism effect as '22' in the manuscript held at PubMed Central, which cannot be right beside r = .11, so that figure is left out and the F and r are quoted instead. Searches for an experiment on the fallacy covered Europe PMC, Crossref, the four fallacy reference works named above, and open web search under both its names.
misreadings: The first error is to file the fallacy by direction. It is not hasty generalisation, which builds a rule from too few cases, and it is not the fallacy of accident, which pushes a rule onto a case its exceptions cover. Fischer's target has its exceptions stated on the page, which is what makes it hard to answer: every word of it is true. The second error is to treat it as a claim about lying. The overwhelming exception is a fault of proportion between what a sentence says and what it is used to suggest, and Fischer's charge against Woodward is that the thesis survived revision by shedding its content, not that anything in it was false. The third is to take the stock examples for Fischer's. The Monty Python line and Henry Ford's black paint come from the fallacy lists, and Ford's sentence is a joke about a real policy rather than an argument at all. Fischer's own cases are a parody history of Magna Carta and two working historians. The fourth error is to read the reader-side experiments as vindication. What van der Bles and colleagues show is that an explicit statement of uncertainty does reach people, while the word 'estimated' or the word 'around' does not, so the danger runs to qualifiers too small to notice rather than to qualifications that are spelled out. The last is to conclude that caveats are free. Communicating uncertainty in those studies cut trust in the number itself, d = -0.34, and the cut was driven by the verbal statements that worked.

sources.text: Fischer, D. H. (1970). Historians' Fallacies: Toward a Logic of Historical Thought. New York: Harper & Row. Read as the Internet Archive OCR text, downloaded twice with identical checksums. Source for the definition on page 127, the 1066 and All That and Bjork examples, the Woodward footnote at page 149, and the index of fallacies.
Wikipedia, Overwhelming exception. Read as the article wikitext. Used to find Fischer, and quoted here as the carrier of the definition and the examples that circulate under the name.
Bennett, B. Overwhelming Exception. Logically Fallacious. Read in full. Source for the logical form and for the wording shared with the Wikipedia definition.
Copi, I. M., Cohen, C., & McMahon, K. Introduction to Logic, Fourteenth Edition. Pearson Education Limited, 2014. Read as text extracted from this PDF and searched whole for the phrase.
Dowden, B. Fallacies. Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. Downloaded and searched whole; the phrase does not occur.
Hansen, H. Fallacies. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. Downloaded and searched whole; neither the phrase nor Fischer's name occurs.
Curtis, G. N. Taxonomy of Logical Fallacies. The Fallacy Files. The taxonomy page was downloaded and searched; the phrase does not occur on it.

van der Bles, A. M., van der Linden, S., Freeman, A. L. J., & Spiegelhalter, D. J. (2020). The effects of communicating uncertainty on public trust in facts and numbers. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 117(14), 7672-7683. Every figure quoted was read from the JATS XML at PubMed Central, PMC7149229, downloaded twice with identical checksums.

How readers understand causal and correlational expressions used in news headlines. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied, 23(1), 1-14. Read as the author manuscript posted at gwern.net, which predates the correction that restored the fourth author.

"How readers understand causal and correlational expressions used in news headlines": Correction to Adams et al. (2016). Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied, 23(1), 28. Read as the PubMed record, PMID 27936831. It restores an omitted author and an acknowledgement, and reports no change to any result.

Including limitations in news coverage of cancer research: Effects of news hedging on fatalism, medical skepticism, patient trust, and backlash. Journal of Health Communication, 16(5), 486-503. Read as the author manuscript at PubMed Central, PMC9426780.

Information, Communication & Society, 23(1), 128-147. Closed at the publisher, with no repository copy recorded by Unpaywall; its figures are quoted only as the 2022 paper reports them.

Named as existing; closed at the publisher, with no repository copy recorded by Unpaywall, and nothing from it is quoted here.
